title: Laute II: ch, ß und das deutsche r
summary: The two ch sounds, the letter ß, the throaty r, and the letters that trick English eyes

blocks.title: One spelling, two ch sounds
blocks.body: *ch* is really **two** sounds. The **soft** one (the "ich-Laut") is a gentle hiss, like a cat: *ich* (I), *echt* (really), *Küche* (kitchen). The **hard** one (the "ach-Laut") is a scrape at the back of the throat, like gently clearing it: *Bach* (stream), *Buch* (book), *auch* (also). **The rule is automatic:** after *a, o, u, au* you get the hard scrape; everywhere else, the soft hiss.
blocks.callout: You don't choose — the vowel before it decides for you.

blocks.title: Tap to hear both ch sounds

pairs.note: After a, o, u, au it's the throaty one. Everywhere else, the gentle hiss.

blocks.prompt: Which word has the HARD 'ach' scrape (back of the throat)?
blocks.explain: *Buch* — after *u*, the *ch* is the hard scrape. After *i/e* (*ich, echt*) it's the soft hiss.

blocks.title: The letter ß (Eszett)
blocks.body: **ß** is called the *Eszett* or *scharfes S* — a single, sharp, voiceless "s". It only appears **after a long vowel or a diphthong**: *Fuß* (foot), *Straße* (street), *heißen* (to be called). After a **short** vowel you write **ss** instead: *Fluss* (river), *muss* (must). Switzerland drops ß altogether, but in Germany it's standard.
blocks.callout: ß never starts a word, and never follows a short vowel.

blocks.title: Letters that trick English eyes
blocks.body: The German **r** lives at the **back of the throat** — a soft gargle, not an English roll: *rot* (red), *Frau* (woman). And four letters flip what you expect: **w** sounds like English *v* (*Wasser* = VASS-er), **v** usually sounds like *f* (*Vater* = FAH-ter), **z** is *ts* (*Zeit* = TSITE), and **j** is *y* (*ja* = YAH).

blocks.prompt: Listen and type what you hear.
Type the German for 'foot' — long vowel, so it takes ß.
blocks.hint: Sharp s after a long u.
blocks.explain: *Fuß* — the *u* is long, so it's ß, not ss.

blocks.prompt: Which consonant surprised you most — w, v, z, j, or the throaty r? Write three German words that use a ch or a ß.
